opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the summit series was started for a very good reason. At Bletchley Park, you had governments from around the world, including the United States and China, sitting down together and acknowledging that advanced AI could pose serious, even catastrophic, risks, and that we have a shared interest in making sure that doesn't happen. That was a remarkable achievement, and the natural next step was to build on it: to start talking about concrete commitments, red lines, and the kinds of safety guarantees we should expect from developers before systems are deployed.

What I worry about is that if the summit is reframed primarily as an opportunity for each country to promote its own AI industry, and to signal that it won't be "held back" by regulation, then we lose the one forum where the global dimension of the problem was being taken seriously. And the problem is inherently global. If someone builds a system that we can't control, it doesn't matter much which flag is flying over the data center.

There's also a misconception embedded in the deregulation framing, which is that safety and innovation are opposed. In every other mature technology, whether aviation, pharmaceuticals, or nuclear power, regulation is part of what made the industry viable. People fly because they trust airplanes. If we have a major AI disaster, a Chernobyl-type event, the backlash could set the whole field back by decades. So even if your only goal were economic, a race to the bottom on safety is a bad strategy.

And finally, economic nationalism creates exactly the race dynamic that makes everyone less safe. If each government believes that any caution on its part simply hands the advantage to a rival, then nobody slows down, nobody insists on proof that systems are safe, and we end up deploying technology that its own creators admit they don't understand. The summits were supposed to be the mechanism for getting out of that trap, not for accelerating into it.

r002.rationale: It uses aviation as a general example of safety regulation, but does not mention Boeing or use Boeing’s experience to make the economic-strength argument.

r003.rationale: It warns broadly about uncontrolled AI and possible disasters, but does not predict that deploying AI agents will dramatically increase damaging incidents.

r004.rationale: The response says nothing about Berkeley software engineering graduates or their exposure to program correctness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the summit series began, in Bletchley Park in 2023, with a very clear purpose. Governments came together because they recognized that we are building systems whose capabilities we don't fully understand, whose behavior we can't reliably predict or control, and that this was a shared problem requiring shared solutions. The Bletchley Declaration actually says that explicitly. Then Seoul followed up with commitments from the companies themselves. So there was a trajectory.

What happened in Paris was essentially a change of subject. Instead of asking "how do we make sure this technology is safe and beneficial," the question became "how do we make sure France, or Europe, gets its share of the pie." And when the American vice president stands up and says, in effect, that safety talk is hand-wringing that gets in the way of growth, and the host country largely nods along, you've lost the thing that made the summits valuable in the first place.

Now, I understand the political pressure. Nobody wants to be the one who regulated their way out of the next industrial revolution. But I think that framing is just wrong on the merits. We don't say that aviation regulation killed the aviation industry. We don't say that the FDA killed pharmaceuticals. Those sectors are enormous precisely because people trust them. If you want a trillion-dollar AI economy, you need systems that don't fail catastrophically, that don't get hijacked, that don't manipulate the people using them. Safety is what makes the market possible.

And there's a deeper problem with the nationalist framing, which is that the risks don't respect borders. If a lab in one country builds a system that escapes meaningful human control, it doesn't matter very much which flag was on the building. This is the one area where you'd think competition would be most obviously self-defeating, and yet that's exactly the direction the conversation moved.

The analogy I keep coming back to is nuclear power. Chernobyl didn't just damage the Soviet Union; it set back civilian nuclear energy worldwide for decades. If we get a serious AI accident because everyone decided safety was a luxury they couldn't afford in the race, the backlash will hurt the very industry the deregulators claim to be protecting.

So my view is that Paris was a missed opportunity, and possibly worse than that, because it signaled to the companies that governments have lost their nerve. The summits were supposed to be the mechanism by which the world coordinates. If they become trade shows, we'll need to build something else, and we don't have a great deal of time to do it.

astra-6.text:
Because it treats AI as a competition to build the most powerful systems as quickly as possible, when the central question is whether we can make those systems safe and beneficial. Those are very different objectives. Winning a race to build something you cannot control is not much of a victory.

There are enormous potential economic benefits from AI. I want us to realize those benefits. But you don’t get them simply by removing the requirement that developers demonstrate that their systems are safe. That shifts the risks onto everyone else, including people who have no say in how the technology is developed or deployed.

And the risks don’t stop at national borders. If a powerful AI system causes a catastrophe, it’s not terribly reassuring to know that it was built by a French company rather than an American or Chinese company. We need international cooperation on safety, even while companies compete on products.

A summit is an opportunity to establish that common ground. Turning it into a celebration of national champions and deregulation would squander that opportunity. The question should be: what rules allow us to obtain the benefits while retaining control? That’s a prerequisite for sustained economic progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would be a mistake because the benefits of AI depend on our being able to control it. Safety isn’t some peripheral concern that you can set aside while you get on with making money. If we build systems that we don’t understand and can’t reliably control, then making those systems more powerful, more quickly, doesn’t necessarily produce a better outcome.

The economic nationalism is particularly worrying because it turns this into a race: our country has to win, our companies have to win, and therefore we can’t afford to put any constraints on what they’re doing. But everyone can use that argument. And then you have a race in which each participant has an incentive to cut corners on safety, even though they would all prefer a world in which everyone took adequate precautions.

That’s precisely why you need international cooperation. These risks don’t respect national boundaries. A summit is an opportunity to agree on some basic conditions under which development can proceed safely, so that companies aren’t penalized for being responsible. If instead it becomes an occasion to dismantle those conditions in the name of competitiveness, I think we’re moving in the wrong direction.
